topic.title: Your trip is the nine photos you posted
topic.claim: You come back with hundreds of trip photos and post a handful, and years later the handful is the trip you remember.
topic.moment: Back from a trip with 1,400 photos; you spend an evening choosing nine, the ones where everyone looks like they're having the time you meant to have.

turn.actually: You're choosing which version of it you'll keep. The nine you posted are the ones you'll scroll back to, and they slowly replace the rest.

topic.because: The photos you look at again are the moments you keep revisiting; the 1,391 in the gallery you never open again. The fight at the airport and the rainy day aren't in the nine, so a few years on they barely exist.
topic.payoff: You didn't post the trip. You picked the one you'll remember.
topic.send_to: the friend who took all the photos on your last trip
topic.group: anyone who has posted trip photos

cover.headline: You posted nine photos. They [became the whole trip]
cover.sub: The rest you never open again.

paragraphs: You posted nine photos from the trip. A few years on, those nine are the only trip you remember.
slides.why_swipe: How could nine photos be the whole trip?

paragraphs: You're back home, bag still half unpacked, hundreds of photos sitting on your phone.
You spend the evening on the sofa, swiping. You pick the nine where everyone looks like they're having the time you meant to have. Crop one, pick a caption, post.
Felt like sharing it with everyone who wasn't there.
slides.why_swipe: If not sharing, then what were you doing?

paragraphs: But those nine are the ones you'll scroll back to. The rest sit under *Recents*, and nobody opens Recents again.
Memory keeps whatever you keep looking at. So the fight at the airport and the rainy day stuck inside slowly stop existing.
slides.why_swipe: So is the posted version a lie?

paragraphs: It's not a lie. Those nine moments really happened, and you really were that happy in them.
The trip just got edited down to one good evening on the sofa, by you.
slides.why_swipe: So what did posting really do?

paragraphs: **You didn't post the trip. You picked the one you'll remember.**
Open your camera roll right now, scroll past the nine, and meet the trip you forgot you took.

end.save: Come back to it the next time you sit down to choose which photos to post.
end.send: Send it to the friend who took every photo on your last trip.
end.promise: How the internet edits your life.

claims.text: Repeated viewing of a specific photo or moment reinforces and strengthens the memory of it.
claims.sentence: Memory keeps whatever you keep looking at.

claims.text: Moments or events that are not revisited/looked at again gradually fade from memory, to the point of effectively ceasing to be remembered.
claims.sentence: So the fight at the airport and the rainy day stuck inside slowly stop existing.

claims.text: As a result of this selective reinforcement, the small set of posted, repeatedly-viewed photos becomes the entirety of a person's remembered trip years later, replacing the memory of the whole trip.
claims.sentence: A few years on, those nine are the only trip you remember.

ledger.sentence: Memory keeps whatever you keep looking at.

ledger.text: Moments or events that are not revisited/looked at again gradually fade from memory, to the point of effectively ceasing to be remembered.
ledger.sentence: So the fight at the airport and the rainy day stuck inside slowly stop existing.

ledger.text: As a result of this selective reinforcement, the small set of posted, repeatedly-viewed photos becomes the entirety of a person's remembered trip years later, replacing the memory of the whole trip.
ledger.sentence: A few years on, those nine are the only trip you remember.

mechanism.broken_premise: None breaks. Premise 2 is overstated in degree: unrevisited memories lose accessibility and can become effectively unrecoverable, but the mechanism suppresses/weakens rather than literally deleting the trace.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Looking at the posted photos again is retrieval practice, which strengthens those specific memories (the testing effect and Henkel's finding that actively reviewing photos aids memory). Crucially, selectively retrieving part of an experience actively inhibits the related parts you don't revisit — 'retrieval-induced forgetting' (Anderson, Bjork & Bjork, 1994) — so the un-posted moments don't merely decay, they get suppressed. Over years the repeatedly-viewed nine therefore dominate and come to stand in for the whole trip, exactly as the post claims, with the only caveat that the faded moments are made inaccessible rather than erased.

sources.quote: retrieving a subset of items from a category caused the forgetting of other items from that category... this effect apparently reflects inhibition that occurs as a by-product of memory retrieval
Retrieval-induced forgetting denotes the phenomenon that selectively retrieving only a subset of information from memory lowers the accessibility of the non-retrieved rest of that set.
photos might help museum-goers remember their trip in the long term, but only if they actively review and interact with the pictures rather than just amass them
